title: Chapter 1.  Geography — The Imphal Valley & Surrounding Hills

blocks.content: Manipur's geography is defined by a single, exam-critical structural fact: a small, fertile, oval-shaped central valley (home to the majority of the state's population) surrounded on all sides by extensive hill ranges (home to most of its tribal population) - a valley-versus-hills divide that underlies almost every other chapter of this book, from demography to the state's recent history.

Manipur lies in India's north-east, bordered by Nagaland to the north, Mizoram to the south, Assam to the west, and Myanmar (Burma) to the east - making it one of only a few Indian states sharing an international border with Myanmar, a fact with significant implications for its trade, security and ethnic-demographic profile (Chapters 8, 12).

The state's geography is sharply divided into two contrasting zones: the Imphal Valley (also called the Manipur Valley) - a small, flat, fertile, oval-shaped lowland roughly 700 m above sea level at the state's centre, covering only about one-tenth of the state's total area - and the surrounding hill ranges, which make up roughly nine-tenths of Manipur's land area, encircling the valley on all sides.

This valley-hills geographic divide closely (though not perfectly) tracks Manipur's ethnic-demographic divide: the Imphal Valley is predominantly inhabited by the Meitei community (Manipur's largest single ethnic group, mostly Hindu with a Sanamahi/indigenous-faith minority), while the surrounding hills are predominantly inhabited by various recognised Scheduled Tribe communities, broadly grouped into Naga and Kuki-Zo ethnic-linguistic clusters (Chapter 8) - a demographic pattern of direct and central relevance to understanding the state's political history and recent developments (Chapter 12).

cells: Central, oval-shaped, fertile lowland; approx one-tenth of the state's area; average elevation approx 790 m
Surround the valley on all sides; approx nine-tenths of the state's area

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: The Imphal Valley covers only about 10% of Manipur's total land area but contains the large majority of the state's population - while the surrounding hills cover roughly 90% of the land area but are comparatively sparsely populated. This valley-vs-hills area/population INVERSION is one of the most frequently tested geography-cum-demography facts about Manipur.

Loktak Lake, in the southern part of the Imphal Valley, is the largest freshwater lake in North-East India and one of the most distinctive wetland ecosystems in the country, famous for its 'phumdis' - floating masses of vegetation, soil and organic matter that dot the lake's surface, some large and stable enough to support human habitation and cultivation.

The lake hosts Keibul Lamjao National Park, the world's only floating national park, situated entirely on phumdis and forming the last natural habitat of the Sangai (Manipur brown-antlered deer, Chapter 9) - making Loktak Lake one of Manipur's most ecologically and symbolically significant sites, and a designated Ramsar wetland of international importance.

★ EXAM POINT: Keibul Lamjao National Park (on Loktak Lake) is described as the world's ONLY floating national park - a globally unique geographical superlative and one of the most frequently tested facts about Manipur.

items: The Imphal River, Iril River, and Thoubal River are among the principal rivers draining the Imphal Valley, eventually feeding into Loktak Lake or the wider Manipur river system.
The Barak River, Manipur's most significant river by volume, rises in the state's hills and flows westward into Assam and eventually Bangladesh, forming part of the wider Surma-Meghna river system.

Manipur's climate is sub-tropical highland/monsoon in character, with the hills experiencing cooler temperatures than the valley; the state receives substantial rainfall from the South-West monsoon, supporting its extensive forest cover in the hill districts.
Manipur: approx 22,327 sq km; borders Nagaland, Mizoram, Assam, and Myanmar (international border); capital: Imphal.
Imphal Valley = ~10% of the state's area but home to the majority of the population (predominantly Meitei); surrounding hills = ~90% of the area (predominantly Naga and Kuki-Zo tribal communities).
Loktak Lake = largest freshwater lake in North-East India; famous for its floating 'phumdis'.
Keibul Lamjao National Park (on Loktak Lake) = the world's ONLY floating national park; last natural habitat of the Sangai deer.
Barak River = Manipur's most significant river by volume, flows into Assam and the wider Surma-Meghna system.
